title: Jupiter: The Giant Planet That Could Hold 1,300 Earths
summary:
Imagine a planet so big that more than 1,300 Earths could fit inside it. That's Jupiter, the giant of our solar system. Some astronomers call it a failed star because it's mostly hydrogen and helium — the same stuff stars are made of.

If you tried to land on Jupiter, you'd be in trouble. There's no solid ground! You'd sink through clouds of ammonia and water vapor until the pressure crushed you. Science fiction writers have suggested exploring it in hot-air balloons, but orbiting safely above is a much better idea.

Jupiter's clouds whip around at more than 300 miles per hour. Its most famous feature is the Great Red Spot — a hurricane that's been raging for centuries. Nearly three Earths could fit across it!

Jupiter also has nearly 70 moons. Ganymede is bigger than Mercury and has its own magnetic field. Io is the most volcanic place in the solar system, shooting sulfur clouds 300 miles high. And Europa? It's covered in ice, but scientists think a liquid ocean might hide beneath — and maybe even life.

One more weird fact: Jupiter is the largest planet, but it has the shortest day. It spins so fast that a day lasts only 10 hours. Now that's a quick spin!
why_it_matters: Studying giant planets like Jupiter helps scientists figure out how our solar system formed, and its icy moon Europa is one of the best places to hunt for life beyond Earth.

background_read: Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun and the biggest one — it is so enormous that every other planet could fit inside it.
Mercury (the smallest planet and the one closest to the Sun) is smaller than Jupiter's moon Ganymede, which shows just how huge Jupiter's family of moons is.
The astronomer Galileo Galilei spotted Jupiter's four biggest moons with one of the first telescopes around 1610 — the first time anyone had seen moons circling another planet.
Article_Structure: WHO: Astronomers who study Jupiter, plus science fiction writers who imagined exploring it in hot-air balloons.
WHAT: The article explains Jupiter's size (1,300 Earths could fit inside), its hydrogen and helium makeup, its 300-mile-per-hour clouds, its Great Red Spot storm, and its nearly 70 moons.
WHERE: Jupiter sits in our solar system, with moons like Ganymede, Io, and Europa — Europa is covered in ice with a possible ocean hiding beneath.
WHY: Learning about Jupiter helps us understand how planets work and whether a hidden ocean on Europa could ever support life.

perspectives.description: Jupiter is a record-breaker — biggest planet, shortest day, most volcanic moon — which makes it one of the most exciting places in the solar system to learn about.
Anyone hoping to visit Jupiter would face crushing pressure and no solid ground, so even science fiction's balloon idea is risky — orbiting safely above is far better.
Researchers are most interested in Europa, where a hidden liquid ocean beneath the ice might hold the right conditions for living things.
